Determined to keep his principality, which an old prophecy says he will lose, Manfred decides to divorce his wife and marry his dead son's bride, Isabella, who flees through the underground passages of the castle, while portraits step out of their frames and a giant figure in armour appears.
context: Published in 1764 as the translation of an old Italian manuscript, The Castle of Otranto was in fact written by Horace Walpole (1717–1797), son of the British prime minister and builder of a famous mock-Gothic house at Strawberry Hill. It is considered the first Gothic novel, the ancestor of [Dracula](/book/139?lang=en) and [Frankenstein](/book/137?lang=en). Walpole also invented the word serendipity.

about: Thomas De Quincey tells how, at seventeen, he ran away from school, wandered in Wales and lived homeless in London, where he was saved from collapse by a young street girl named Ann, whom he lost and never found again. Years later, a student at Oxford, he first took opium for pain, and he describes, with great honesty, its early pleasures and then its torments, above all the enormous dreams of architecture, oceans and the East.
context: First published in 1821, it was the first great memoir of addiction in English, and a warning as much as a confession. De Quincey (1785–1859) was a friend of [Wordsworth](/author/wordsworth?lang=en) and Coleridge and one of the finest essayists of his time. Its long, musical sentences are a pleasure in themselves.

about: During the American Civil War, a Southern planter named Peyton Farquhar stands on a railway bridge in Alabama with a rope around his neck, about to be hanged by Union soldiers for trying to sabotage the line. The rope breaks, he falls into the river, and the story follows his desperate escape through the water and the forest toward his wife and home.
context: Ambrose Bierce (1842–c. 1914) fought in some of the bloodiest battles of the war and wrote about it without illusion. Published in 1890, this short story is famous for its ending, which has influenced films and writers ever since; read it without spoilers. Bierce, author of the satirical Devil's Dictionary, disappeared in Mexico during its revolution and was never found. Compare [The Red Badge of Courage](/book/442?lang=en).

about: Aubrey, a romantic young Englishman, travels across Europe with the mysterious Lord Ruthven, a pale nobleman who fascinates London society and seems to bring ruin to everyone he favours. In Greece a girl Aubrey loves is killed by a vampire; soon after, Ruthven is mortally wounded and makes Aubrey swear to keep silent about him for a year. Back in London, Aubrey sees him again.
context: The story was born in 1816 at the Villa Diodati by Lake Geneva, in the same ghost-story contest that produced [Frankenstein](/book/137?lang=en). John William Polidori (1795–1821), [Byron](/author/byron?lang=en)'s young doctor, developed it from a fragment by Byron, and it was first published in 1819 under Byron's name by mistake. It created the aristocratic vampire that led to Dracula.

about: During the carnival season in an Italian city, Montresor meets his enemy Fortunato, a proud wine expert who is already a little drunk. Pretending to need his opinion on a cask of rare Amontillado sherry, Montresor leads him down into the damp family catacombs beneath his palazzo, deeper and deeper among the bones, toward a revenge he has planned with great care.
context: Published in 1846, this short tale is one of Edgar Allan Poe's most perfect, told by the murderer himself half a century later, and it never says what insult started it all. It takes only a few minutes to read and is impossible to forget. See [Poe's life](/author/poe?lang=en) and his [Fall of the House of Usher](/book/128?lang=en).

about: While a plague called the Red Death empties his country, Prince Prospero shuts himself away with a thousand knights and ladies in a fortified abbey, determined to enjoy himself. Six months later he gives a masked ball in a suite of seven rooms, each decorated in a single colour; the last is black, lit through blood-red windows, and holds a great ebony clock whose chimes stop the dancers cold. At midnight, a new guest appears.
context: Published in 1842, the tale is a short, dreamlike allegory about the impossibility of escaping death, and it has been read anew in every age of epidemics. Its colours and rhythms show Poe's skill as a poet in prose. Read it with [The Cask of Amontillado](/book/1319?lang=en).

about: A geologist from Miskatonic University tells why he is begging the world not to send another expedition to Antarctica. His team, flying over unexplored mountains higher than the Himalayas, discovered the ruins of a colossal city built long before humanity by star-born beings, and learned from its carvings the history of the Earth, and of the things that had destroyed its makers.
context: Lovecraft wrote this short novel in 1931, but it was rejected and only appeared in 1936 in a science fiction magazine. Its mix of scientific detail and cosmic dread makes it one of his most admired works, an influence on later science fiction and horror films. Begin with [The Call of Cthulhu](/book/62316?lang=en).

about: In the decaying hill country of Massachusetts lives the Whateley family: a half-mad old farmer, his albino daughter and her son Wilbur, who grows at an unnatural rate, is nearly a man at ten, and comes to the library of Miskatonic University to consult a forbidden book. When dogs attack him there, the librarian discovers that Wilbur is not entirely human, and that something even larger is hidden in the Whateley farmhouse.
context: Published in 1929, The Dunwich Horror is one of Lovecraft's most exciting stories. The forbidden book is his invented Necronomicon, which he attributed to an imaginary 'mad Arab' named Abdul Alhazred, a sign of how the East fascinated him. See [The Call of Cthulhu](/book/62316?lang=en).

about: When her father, a country clergyman, leaves the Church over a matter of conscience, Margaret Hale must leave her beloved village in the green south of England for Milton, a smoky cotton-manufacturing town in the north. There she clashes with the proud mill owner John Thornton, befriends a union leader's dying daughter, and finds herself in the middle of a strike that tests everyone's ideas about masters and workers.
context: Elizabeth Gaskell published North and South in Dickens's magazine in 1854 and 1855, and it is both a love story in the tradition of [Pride and Prejudice](/book/38?lang=en) and a serious novel about industrial England. Gaskell, a minister's wife who lived in Manchester, knew the subject well. Her gentler [Cranford](/book/697?lang=en) is also in the library.

about: Silas Marner, a linen weaver falsely accused of theft by his religious community, settles in the village of Raveloe and lives alone for fifteen years, weaving and counting the gold he hoards. One night his gold is stolen. Soon after, on New Year's Eve, a little girl with golden hair toddles into his cottage from the snow, where her mother lies dead, and Silas decides to raise her.
context: Published in 1861, this short novel is George Eliot's most fable-like book, a story about how love can bring a lonely man back to life, and about the secret that one of the village's leading men is keeping. It is the best introduction to Eliot before [Middlemarch](/book/490?lang=en) and [The Mill on the Floss](/book/6692?lang=en).

about: Maggie Tulliver is a dark-haired, clever, passionate girl growing up at Dorlcote Mill on the river Floss, adoring her stern brother Tom, who never approves of her. When their father loses the mill in a lawsuit, the family falls into poverty, and Maggie, torn between loyalty to her family and her own heart, is drawn first to the crippled son of her father's enemy and later to her cousin's charming suitor.
context: Published in 1860, it is George Eliot's most autobiographical novel: like Maggie, she was a gifted girl whose beloved brother cut her off when she broke with convention. Its picture of childhood is one of the finest in English, and its ending is famous. Read [Middlemarch](/book/490?lang=en) for Eliot's broadest canvas.

about: Two young women leave Miss Pinkerton's academy on the same day: gentle, wealthy Amelia Sedley and her friend Becky Sharp, a penniless orphan with green eyes, a sharp wit and no intention of staying poor. While the armies gather for the Battle of Waterloo, Becky climbs through English society by charm and lies, and Amelia clings to her love for a vain young officer.
context: William Makepeace Thackeray (1811–1863), born in Calcutta, published the novel in monthly parts in 1847 and 1848 with his own illustrations, and called it 'a novel without a hero'. The title comes from the fair of worldly vanities in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress. Becky Sharp is one of the most delightful bad heroines in fiction.

about: In 1799, during the storming of Seringapatam in India, an English officer steals a great yellow diamond from a Hindu shrine. Fifty years later it is left to his niece, Rachel Verinder, as a birthday present, and on the night of her birthday it disappears from her room. Three mysterious Indians have been seen near the house, and the famous Sergeant Cuff is called in.
context: Published in 1868, The Moonstone is told by several witnesses, including a house steward who consults [Robinson Crusoe](/book/300?lang=en) for advice on every occasion. T. S. Eliot called it the first, the longest and the best of modern English detective novels. Wilkie Collins also wrote [The Woman in White](/book/880?lang=en).

about: In May 1914 Richard Hannay, a mining engineer just back from Africa and bored with London, lets a frightened neighbour into his flat. The man, an American named Scudder, claims to have uncovered a German plot to steal British war plans, involving a secret group called the Black Stone. A few days later Hannay finds him dead on the floor with a knife through his heart, and flees north to the moors of Scotland, chased by both the police and the spies.
context: John Buchan (1875–1940) wrote the novel in late 1914 while recovering from illness, and published it in 1915; it created the modern thriller of the innocent man on the run, later perfected in Alfred Hitchcock's 1935 film. Buchan was also a historian, a politician and Governor General of Canada. For an older adventure across the Highlands, read [Kidnapped](/book/187?lang=en).

about: In 1792, at the height of the Terror in revolutionary Paris, a mysterious Englishman known only by his sign, a small red flower called the scarlet pimpernel, keeps smuggling condemned aristocrats out of France under the noses of the guards. In London, the beautiful Marguerite Blakeney is married to Sir Percy, the richest and silliest fop in society, and she is blackmailed by a French agent into helping him unmask the Pimpernel.
context: Baroness Emmuska Orczy (1865–1947), born in Hungary and raised in London, first wrote the story as a play in 1903 and then as a novel in 1905. Sir Percy, the hero who hides behind a foolish public face, became the model for Zorro and many later masked heroes. It is fast, romantic and pure entertainment.

about: England, 1194: King Richard the Lionheart is a prisoner abroad, his brother Prince John rules, and the Norman lords oppress the Saxons. Wilfred of Ivanhoe, disinherited by his Saxon father for following Richard on Crusade, returns in disguise and fights in a great tournament. Around him gather the outlaw Robin of Locksley, a mysterious Black Knight, the Saxon princess Rowena and the brave Rebecca, daughter of the Jewish moneylender Isaac of York.
context: Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832), the Scottish poet and lawyer often called the father of the historical novel, published Ivanhoe in 1819, and it shaped the popular image of the Middle Ages for a century. Its portrait of Rebecca and the prejudice she faces is the moral heart of the book. Arab readers may also seek out Scott's The Talisman, which shows Saladin as a wise and noble ruler.

about: In 1757, during the war between Britain and France for North America, the scout Hawkeye and his Mohican friends Chingachgook and his son Uncas guide two sisters, Cora and Alice Munro, through the forests of upstate New York to their father, the commander of Fort William Henry. Their journey is shadowed by Magua, a Huron warrior with his own reasons for revenge, and the fort's fall leads to a massacre.
context: James Fenimore Cooper (1789–1851) published the novel in 1826, the second of his five Leatherstocking Tales about Hawkeye, and it became one of the first American bestsellers. Its view of Native Americans mixes admiration with the stereotypes of its time. The 1992 film introduced it to new readers.

about: Black Beauty tells his own story, from a happy colthood in an English meadow through service with kind and cruel owners, a terrible night ride to fetch a doctor, the pain of the tight 'bearing rein' that fashionable owners used to keep horses' heads high, and hard years pulling a cab through the streets of London, alongside his friends Ginger and Merrylegs.
context: Anna Sewell (1820–1878), who was disabled after a childhood accident and depended on horses to get around, wrote the book in her last years, dictating much of it to her mother; she died a few months after it was published in 1877. She wrote it to teach kindness to animals, and it changed attitudes to horses across the world. It remains a moving read for children and adults.

about: Heidi, a five-year-old orphan, is taken by her aunt to live with her grandfather, a gruff old man who has cut himself off from the village and lives alone high on a Swiss mountain. Heidi's joy wins him over, and she spends happy days with Peter the goatherd in the meadows. Then she is taken to Frankfurt to be a companion to Clara, a rich girl who cannot walk, and grows so homesick for the mountains that she begins to sleepwalk.
context: Johanna Spyri (1827–1901) grew up in a village above Lake Zurich and published Heidi in two parts in 1880 and 1881. Its picture of the healing power of nature and kindness has made it one of the most read children's books in the world, adapted countless times, including the much-loved Japanese animated series.

about: Mole is spring-cleaning when he suddenly throws down his brush and goes out into the sunshine, where he meets Water Rat, who introduces him to life on the river and the joy of 'messing about in boats'. Through the seasons they visit the wise, gruff Badger in the Wild Wood and their rich, boastful friend Toad, whose passion for motor cars lands him in prison, while weasels take over Toad Hall.
context: Kenneth Grahame (1859–1932) worked at the Bank of England, rising to become its secretary, and the book grew from bedtime stories for his son. Published in 1908, it mixes comic adventure with passages of almost mystical beauty about nature and friendship. It is a classic to read aloud, and adults often love it even more than children.

about: Rudolf Rassendyll, an idle English gentleman, takes a holiday in the small kingdom of Ruritania just before the coronation of its king, who happens to be his distant cousin and his exact double. When the king is drugged on the eve of the ceremony by his ambitious half-brother Black Michael, Rassendyll is persuaded to take his place, and finds himself in a web of intrigue, swordfights and an impossible love for the king's betrothed, Princess Flavia.
context: Anthony Hope (1863–1933), a London lawyer, published the novel in 1894 and it was an instant success, giving its name to a whole genre of adventure stories set in imaginary European kingdoms. Its witty villain, Rupert of Hentzau, almost steals the book. It is a quick, elegant swashbuckler.

about: The elephant hunter Allan Quatermain is hired by Sir Henry Curtis and Captain Good to find Sir Henry's brother, who vanished while searching for the legendary diamond mines of King Solomon. With an old map drawn in blood, they cross a desert and mountains into a hidden kingdom ruled by a cruel king and an ancient witch, and their servant Umbopa turns out to be more than he seems.
context: H. Rider Haggard (1856–1925), who had worked as a young colonial official in southern Africa, wrote the novel in 1885 after betting his brother he could write a book as exciting as [Treasure Island](/book/185?lang=en). It created the lost-world adventure, though its colonial outlook belongs to its time. Haggard's [She](/book/3281?lang=en) is equally famous.

about: A Cambridge scholar, Horace Holly, raises his ward Leo Vincey, and on Leo's twenty-fifth birthday they open a box containing an ancient potsherd and a family legend. Following it to the east coast of Africa, they reach a hidden kingdom ruled by Ayesha, a queen who has lived for two thousand years, waiting for the return of the man she loved, and whom her people call She-who-must-be-obeyed.
context: Published in 1886 and 1887, She was one of the best-selling novels of its time and influenced fantasy writers for generations; its queen bears the Arabic name Ayesha. Like [King Solomon's Mines](/book/2351?lang=en), it reflects the imperial attitudes of H. Rider Haggard's age, but its themes of immortality, love and power still fascinate.

about: In Hamburg, the impatient Professor Lidenbrock finds a coded note in an old Icelandic manuscript: the alchemist Arne Saknussemm claims to have reached the centre of the Earth through the crater of an extinct volcano. With his nervous nephew Axel and a calm Icelandic guide named Hans, Lidenbrock climbs into the crater and descends through tunnels to an underground sea, giant mushrooms and creatures from prehistoric times.
context: Published in 1864, this is one of Jules Verne's most imaginative novels, mixing the geology of his day with pure adventure, and Axel's fear makes it as funny as it is thrilling. Verne also wrote [Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea](/book/121?lang=en); see [his life](/author/verne?lang=en).

about: Paris, 1482. During the Feast of Fools, the crowd crowns as king of fools the most hideous man in the city, Quasimodo, the deaf, hunchbacked bell-ringer of Notre-Dame. Three men become obsessed with Esmeralda, a young dancer who performs in the square with her goat: Quasimodo, the handsome captain Phoebus, and the archdeacon Claude Frollo, whose desire turns to destructive madness.
context: Victor Hugo published the novel in 1831 partly to save the cathedral and Paris's Gothic buildings, which were then neglected, and its success led to the restoration of Notre-Dame. After the fire of 2019 the book returned to bestseller lists. Hugo's later masterpiece is [Les Misérables](/book/44?lang=en).

about: Siddhartha, the handsome son of a Brahmin in ancient India, leaves his comfortable home with his friend Govinda to search for enlightenment. He lives with wandering ascetics, meets the Buddha himself but decides he must find his own way, and then plunges into the world: love with the courtesan Kamala, wealth as a merchant, and finally disgust. At last, beside a river, a simple ferryman teaches him to listen.
context: Hermann Hesse (1877–1962), a German-Swiss writer whose family had worked as missionaries in India, published Siddhartha in 1922 after his own spiritual crisis. Short and written in calm, lyrical prose, it became a cult book in the 1960s, and Hesse received the Nobel Prize in 1946. Read it beside [Tagore's Sadhana](/book/361?lang=en).

about: Booker T. Washington was born into slavery in Virginia and never knew the date of his birth. After emancipation he worked as a boy in salt furnaces and coal mines, then walked hundreds of miles to Hampton Institute, where he was admitted after cleaning a room so carefully that the teacher could not find a speck of dust. He tells how, in 1881, he founded a school for Black students in Tuskegee, Alabama, which the students built brick by brick.
context: Published in 1901, the autobiography made Washington (1856–1915) the most influential Black leader of his day and preaches self-help and patience. Its cautious approach to civil rights was sharply criticised by W. E. B. Du Bois in [The Souls of Black Folk](/book/710?lang=en). Read it with [Frederick Douglass's Narrative](/book/403?lang=en).

about: In January 1776, more than a year after fighting had begun between Britain and its American colonies, most colonists still hoped for reconciliation with the king. This short pamphlet argued, in plain and forceful language that any farmer or artisan could follow, that monarchy and hereditary rule were absurd, that an island could not govern a continent, and that independence was the only sensible course.
context: Thomas Paine (1737–1809) had arrived in America from England only in 1774, with a letter of recommendation from [Benjamin Franklin](/book/18052?lang=en). Common Sense sold in enormous numbers and helped prepare the way for the Declaration of Independence that July. Paine later defended the French Revolution in Rights of Man. Compare [Locke's Second Treatise](/book/7358?lang=en).

about: In 1787 and 1788, eighty-five essays appeared in New York newspapers under the pen name 'Publius', urging citizens to ratify the new Constitution of the United States. Their authors, Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay, explain the dangers of a weak union, the separation of powers, checks and balances and how a large republic can control factions.
context: The Federalist Papers are still the best guide to how the American Constitution was meant to work and are cited by its courts. Federalist No. 10 on factions and No. 51, with its famous line that 'if men were angels, no government would be necessary', are the most read. For the ideas behind them, see [Locke's Second Treatise](/book/7358?lang=en).

about: In 1831 a young French aristocrat, Alexis de Tocqueville, travelled through the United States for nine months, officially to study its prisons. He came home and wrote this book, which asks how a society built on equality works: its townships and juries, its newspapers and associations, its religion and its laws, and the danger he called the tyranny of the majority.
context: Tocqueville (1805–1859) believed that democracy was the future of Europe too, and wanted to understand its strengths and risks before it arrived. Published in 1835, the first volume is still quoted by politicians and scholars of every persuasion. It pairs naturally with [Mill's On Liberty](/book/264?lang=en), which Tocqueville influenced.

about: Adam Smith begins with a pin factory, where ten workers who divide the task among them make forty-eight thousand pins a day, and from there builds a complete picture of how nations become rich: the division of labour, the role of money and prices, the accumulation of capital, the benefits of free trade, and the duties of government, from defence and justice to education.
context: Published in 1776, The Wealth of Nations founded modern economics, and its line that we expect our dinner not from the benevolence of the butcher but from his regard to his own interest is famous. Smith also criticised monopolies and merchants who conspire against the public. Read it with his [Theory of Moral Sentiments](/book/263?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/smith?lang=en).

about: Can we know anything about the world independently of experience? Kant's answer turns philosophy around: space, time and basic concepts such as cause are not learned from the world but are the forms through which our minds organise every experience. We can therefore know the world as it appears to us with certainty, but never things as they are in themselves, and reason falls into contradictions when it tries.
context: Published in 1781 and revised in 1787, the Critique is one of the most important and most difficult books of philosophy. Kant (see [his life](/author/kant?lang=en)) was answering [David Hume's Enquiry](/book/277?lang=en). New readers might begin with a guide, or with Kant's shorter [Perpetual Peace](/book/157?lang=en).

about: 'The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao.' In eighty-one short chapters, the Tao Te Ching teaches a way of living in harmony with the natural order: yielding like water, which wears away stone; acting without forcing; ruling by not interfering; and valuing simplicity, humility and stillness over ambition and display.
context: Traditionally attributed to [Lao Tzu](/author/laozi?lang=en), the book is one of the most translated texts in the world and the founding scripture of Taoism. This is the classic Victorian translation by James Legge. The chapters are short and can be read one at a time, as a companion to the very different wisdom of [The Analects](/book/258?lang=en).

about: One rainy night in Covent Garden, the phonetics professor Henry Higgins boasts to Colonel Pickering that he could pass off a Cockney flower girl, Eliza Doolittle, as a duchess within six months just by teaching her to speak. Eliza takes him at his word and arrives for lessons, and what begins as a wager becomes a sharp comedy about class, language and a woman who refuses to be anyone's creation.
context: George Bernard Shaw (1856–1950), Irish playwright and critic, wrote Pygmalion in 1912, naming it after the sculptor in Greek myth who fell in love with his statue. He insisted the play should not end in romance. Its musical version, My Fair Lady, became world famous, and Shaw remains one of the few people to have won both a Nobel Prize and an Oscar.

about: Jurgis Rudkus, a strong young Lithuanian immigrant, arrives in Chicago with his family full of hope and finds work in the meatpacking plants of Packingtown. The work is brutal and dangerous, the bosses cheat them, their house is a swindle, and one by one the family is broken by injury, disease and poverty, until Jurgis discovers the socialist movement.
context: Upton Sinclair (1878–1968) wrote the novel after weeks undercover in the stockyards, and its descriptions of filth in the meat plants caused such outrage that Congress passed food safety laws in 1906. Sinclair said he aimed at the public's heart and by accident hit it in the stomach. It is a harrowing book, and an important one.

about: Carol Milford, a lively young librarian full of plans to bring beauty and ideas to the world, marries Will Kennicott, a kind, practical country doctor, and moves to his small town of Gopher Prairie, Minnesota. Its main street, with its ugly shops, gossip and smug contentment, horrifies her, and her efforts to improve the town, through a drama club, new houses or simply different opinions, meet with polite resistance and ridicule.
context: Sinclair Lewis (1885–1951) grew up in just such a town, and the novel's satire of small-town America made it a sensation in 1920. A decade later he became the first American to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. Compare the very different view of the Midwest in [My Ántonia](/book/553?lang=en).

about: In the New York high society of the 1870s, where every gesture is governed by rules, Newland Archer is about to marry the lovely and conventional May Welland. Then May's cousin, Countess Ellen Olenska, returns from Europe after leaving her husband, and her independence and honesty awaken in Newland a longing for a freer life, just as his world closes ranks to keep everyone in their places.
context: Edith Wharton (1862–1937), who was born into that very society, published the novel in 1920 and became the first woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for fiction. Its final scene in Paris is one of the most quietly devastating in American literature. Read also her [Ethan Frome](/book/4598?lang=en) and [The House of Mirth](/book/590?lang=en).

about: In a bleak New England village called Starkfield, a visiting engineer notices a crippled man with a strange look of endurance and pieces together his story. Twenty-four years earlier Ethan Frome, a poor farmer, was trapped in a cold marriage to his sickly wife Zeena, and fell in love with her young cousin Mattie, who had come to help in the house. When Zeena decides to send Mattie away, Ethan has to choose.
context: Published in 1911, this short novel is the starkest thing Edith Wharton wrote, as bare and cold as the winter landscape it describes, and it is often studied for its perfect construction. It is a complete contrast to the glittering drawing rooms of [The Age of Innocence](/book/840?lang=en).

about: Lily Bart is twenty-nine, beautiful, intelligent and without money in New York's richest society, where she must marry well before her looks fade. She is always close to a good match and always, at the last moment, spoils her chances, partly out of pride and partly because she cannot quite make herself sell her life. Her debts, a married man's loan and a jealous rival begin her slow slide down the social ladder.
context: Published in 1905, The House of Mirth was Edith Wharton's first great success; its title comes from the Book of Ecclesiastes, which says that the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. It is a moving and unsparing portrait of a woman with no place in a world that values only money. See also [The Age of Innocence](/book/840?lang=en).

about: Jim Burden, orphaned at ten, travels west by train to live with his grandparents on the Nebraska prairie. On the same train is a family of Bohemian immigrants, and their daughter Ántonia becomes his companion in the vast, windy grassland: they learn English together, kill a rattlesnake and live through a winter in which her father, homesick for the old country, takes his own life.
context: Willa Cather (1873–1947) moved to Nebraska as a child and drew on the immigrant families she knew there. Published in 1918, My Ántonia is a novel of memory, friendship and the land, and one of the great American books about immigrants. Read it with [O Pioneers!](/book/404?lang=en).

about: On the windswept Nebraska prairie, a Swedish immigrant farmer dies and leaves his land to his daughter Alexandra, because she understands it better than his sons. While her neighbours and brothers want to give up and move away, Alexandra believes in the land and makes the farm flourish, but success cannot protect the people she loves, and her youngest brother's secret love ends in tragedy.
context: Published in 1913, O Pioneers! was Willa Cather's first novel of the prairie, and its title comes from a poem by Walt Whitman in [Leaves of Grass](/book/289?lang=en). Cather wrote about strong, independent women and the immigrant families who settled the plains. Continue with [My Ántonia](/book/553?lang=en).

about: Henry Fleming, a young farm boy, enlists in the Union army dreaming of glory. On the eve of his first battle he worries whether he will run, and when the fighting comes he does, fleeing into the woods. Among the wounded on the road he longs for a wound of his own, a red badge of courage, and the story follows his shame and his slow, uncertain return to the fight.
context: Stephen Crane (1871–1900) was born after the Civil War and had never seen a battle when he wrote the novel, which appeared in 1895; veterans praised its truth. It is one of the first great war novels to show fear from the inside. Crane later worked as a war correspondent and died at twenty-eight. Compare [An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge](/book/678?lang=en).

about: A nameless former civil servant, sick and spiteful, writes from his 'underground' corner of St Petersburg. In the first part he rails against the idea that people always act in their own rational interest: humans, he insists, will choose suffering and folly just to prove they are free. In the second part he recalls humiliating episodes from his youth, including a disastrous dinner with old schoolmates and his cruelty to a young woman named Liza.
context: Published in 1864, this short book is often called the first existentialist novel, and its narrator, intelligent and paralysed by his own consciousness, has haunted writers ever since. It opens the way to Dostoevsky's great novels, starting with [Crime and Punishment](/book/12?lang=en). See [Dostoevsky's life](/author/dostoevsky?lang=en).

about: A poor old woodcarver named Geppetto carves a puppet from a piece of wood that can already talk and cry, and the puppet, Pinocchio, runs away almost as soon as he has legs. He is cheated by the Fox and the Cat, hanged from a tree, lured to a land where boys never study and turned into a donkey, and swallowed by an enormous shark, while his nose grows each time he tells a lie.
context: Carlo Collodi was the pen name of Carlo Lorenzini (1826–1890), a Florentine journalist who took his name from his mother's village. Serialised from 1881 to 1883, the story is much darker and stranger than the Disney film, and it is one of the most translated books in the world. Read it with [Alice's Adventures in Wonderland](/book/189?lang=en).

about: Two sisters, Ursula and Gudrun Brangwen, return to their mining town in the English Midlands and become involved with two very different men: Rupert Birkin, a school inspector searching for a new kind of love, and Gerald Crich, the cold, efficient heir to the local coal mines. Their relationships move from the Midlands to the snowy Alps, where passion turns destructive.
context: D. H. Lawrence wrote the novel during the First World War as a sequel to The Rainbow, but publishers were afraid to print it until 1920. It is one of his most ambitious books, full of intense debates about love, industry and modern life. Read [Sons and Lovers](/book/354?lang=en) first, and see [his life](/author/lawrence?lang=en).

about: 'Only connect' is the motto of this novel about three families in Edwardian England: the cultured, idealistic Schlegel sisters, Margaret and Helen; the wealthy, practical Wilcoxes, who run the world's business; and Leonard Bast, a poor clerk who dreams of culture. Their lives become entangled around a country house called Howards End and the question of who will inherit it.
context: Published in 1910, Howards End is E. M. Forster's most ambitious novel about class, money and the future of England, and many critics consider it his masterpiece. It was filmed in 1992. For a lighter Forster, read [A Room with a View](/book/2780?lang=en).

about: In Paris in the 1920s, the American journalist Jake Barnes, wounded in the war, drifts from café to café with a group of expatriate friends and with Lady Brett Ashley, the woman he loves and cannot have. The group travels to Pamplona for the fiesta of San Fermín, with its running of the bulls, and among the drinking and jealousy a young bullfighter becomes the centre of everyone's attention.
context: Ernest Hemingway (1899–1961) published the novel in 1926, and its spare, understated style and its portrait of the 'lost generation' made him famous. He later won the Nobel Prize in 1954. The book entered the public domain in the United States in 2022.

about: In the Hundred Acre Wood live a Bear of Very Little Brain named Winnie-the-Pooh and his friends: the timid Piglet, the gloomy donkey Eeyore, who has lost his tail, the wise-seeming Owl, the busy Rabbit and Kanga and little Roo. Pooh gets stuck in Rabbit's front door after eating too much honey, hunts a Woozle, sets a trap for a Heffalump and joins Christopher Robin on an expedition to the North Pole.
context: A. A. Milne (1882–1956), a playwright and humorist, based the stories on his son Christopher Robin's toy animals, whose originals are now in the New York Public Library, and on the Ashdown Forest near their home. Published in 1926 with E. H. Shepard's drawings, the book entered the public domain in the United States in 2022.

about: A Swiss pastor, his wife and their four sons are shipwrecked on a voyage to the other side of the world and reach a deserted tropical island. Using what they rescue from the wreck and everything the island offers, they build a home in a giant tree, tame animals, plant fields and make, step by step, a comfortable life, with a lesson in natural history or good sense at every turn.
context: The Swiss pastor Johann David Wyss wrote the story for his own sons, and his son Johann Rudolf edited and published it in 1812. Inspired by [Robinson Crusoe](/book/300?lang=en), it turned the castaway tale into a family adventure, and it has been retold and adapted many times since. The natural history is often fanciful, which is part of its charm.

about: 'History is not what you thought. It is what you can remember.' This mock history book takes the reader through English history from the Romans to the First World War in the form in which it survives in the memory of the average schoolboy, complete with 103 Good Things, 5 Bad Kings and 2 Genuine Dates, and absurd examination questions at the end of each chapter.
context: W. C. Sellar and R. J. Yeatman, who had met as students at Oxford, first published their parody in the magazine Punch, and the book appeared in 1930. It is one of the funniest books in English, though the jokes are funniest for readers who know a little English history; it entered the public domain in the United States in 2026.

about: Mr Satterthwaite is an elderly, wealthy man who has always watched life from the sidelines. At a country house party on New Year's Eve, a stranger named Mr Harley Quin appears at the door, and with a few quiet questions helps the guests see the truth about a death that happened years before. In twelve stories Mr Quin appears and vanishes like a figure from a harlequinade, and Mr Satterthwaite becomes his partner.
context: Published in 1930, these stories are unlike Agatha Christie's other mysteries: romantic, a little supernatural and often sad, more about love and fate than about clues. Christie said they were among her favourites. They entered the public domain in the United States in 2026. For Poirot, start with [The Mysterious Affair at Styles](/book/1134?lang=en).

about: Anne Beddingfeld, a young woman tired of a quiet life, is on a London Underground platform when a man falls onto the line and dies. A doctor examines him and hurries away, dropping a scrap of paper with a mysterious message. Following the clue, Anne spends her small inheritance on a passage to South Africa, and finds herself caught up in stolen diamonds, murder and a criminal mastermind known only as the Colonel.
context: Published in 1924, the novel draws on Agatha Christie's own voyage around the British Empire in 1922. It is a light-hearted adventure rather than a classic puzzle, with a brave, funny heroine and chapters from the comic diary of Sir Eustace Pedler, a self-satisfied Member of Parliament. See also [Poirot Investigates](/book/55685?lang=en).

about: Anthony Cade, an adventurer working as a tour guide in southern Africa, agrees to deliver a manuscript of memoirs to a London publisher, and soon finds himself at Chimneys, a great English country house where diplomats are negotiating oil rights for the small Balkan kingdom of Herzoslovakia. A prince is murdered, a famous jewel thief may be among the guests, and the house hides an old secret.
context: Published in 1925, The Secret of Chimneys is one of Agatha Christie's comic thrillers, full of disguises and political intrigue, and it introduces the quiet Superintendent Battle and the lively Lady Eileen 'Bundle' Brent. For a classic Christie puzzle, read [The Murder of Roger Ackroyd](/book/63067?lang=en).

about: This is a selection from the Thousand and One Nights retold for young readers: the frame story of Shahrazad, Aladdin and the wonderful lamp, Ali Baba and the forty thieves, the voyages of Sindbad the sailor, the fisherman and the jinni, the enchanted horse and other tales of magic, merchants and clever servants.
context: Andrew Lang (1844–1912), a Scottish scholar and folklorist, published it in 1898 alongside his famous coloured fairy books. Interestingly, Aladdin and Ali Baba are not found in the old Arabic manuscripts of the Nights: they were added in the eighteenth century by the French translator Antoine Galland, who heard them from a Syrian storyteller, Hanna Diyab. For the complete text, see [Burton's translation](/book/46359?lang=en).

about: In a small shop in Soho that sells cheap stationery and dubious photographs, Mr Verloc lives with his wife Winnie, her ageing mother and her brother Stevie, a gentle young man with a mental disability. Verloc is secretly paid by a foreign embassy to spy on London's anarchists, and when his new employer demands an outrage that will shock the British public, a bomb attack on the Greenwich Observatory, Verloc draws Stevie into the plot, with terrible consequences for everyone in the house.
context: Joseph Conrad based the story on a real incident of 1894, when an anarchist was killed by his own bomb in Greenwich Park. Published in 1907, the novel is darkly ironic and strikingly modern in its picture of terrorism, police and politics, and it inspired Alfred Hitchcock's film Sabotage (1936). Read it with [Heart of Darkness](/book/342?lang=en), and see [Conrad's life](/author/conrad?lang=en).

about: In a New England town stands an old house with seven gables, built by Colonel Pyncheon on land he took from Matthew Maule, a poor man he helped send to the gallows as a wizard. Maule's dying curse seems to hang over the family for two centuries. Now the house shelters the proud, impoverished Hepzibah Pyncheon, who must open a little cent-shop to survive, her broken brother Clifford, just released after a long imprisonment, and a bright young cousin, Phoebe, while their powerful relative Judge Pyncheon schemes in the background.
context: Nathaniel Hawthorne (1804–1864) published the novel in 1851, a year after [The Scarlet Letter](/book/411?lang=en). His own ancestor John Hathorne was a judge at the Salem witch trials, so the theme of inherited guilt was personal to him. The old house in Salem associated with the book can still be visited.

about: In July 1846 Henry David Thoreau spent a night in the jail at Concord, Massachusetts, because for years he had refused to pay a poll tax to a government that allowed slavery and was waging war on Mexico. Someone, probably his aunt, paid the tax, and he was released the next morning against his will. In this essay he explains why: a just person must not lend support to injustice, laws deserve respect only when they are right, and 'under a government which imprisons any unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison'.
context: First given as a lecture and printed in 1849 as Resistance to Civil Government, the essay later inspired Tolstoy, Gandhi in South Africa and India, and Martin Luther King Jr. It can be read in an hour. Thoreau's (1817–1862) great book is [Walden](/book/287?lang=en); see [his life](/author/thoreau?lang=en).

about: Troy has fallen, and the prince Aeneas escapes the burning city carrying his old father on his shoulders and leading his young son by the hand. Destined by the gods to found a new home in Italy, he wanders the Mediterranean for years, is shipwrecked at Carthage, where Queen Dido falls in love with him, and descends into the underworld to meet his father's ghost, before fighting a bitter war in Italy against the hero Turnus.
context: Virgil (70–19 BC) spent the last ten years of his life on the epic, which gave Rome, under the emperor Augustus, a founding story to rival Homer's [Iliad](/book/172?lang=en) and [Odyssey](/book/173?lang=en). He died before finishing it and asked for it to be burned, but Augustus refused. Dido's tragedy in Book IV is one of literature's great love stories, and Dante later chose Virgil as his guide in [The Divine Comedy](/book/170?lang=en).

about: In New York in the 1840s, Catherine Sloper is the plain, shy and kind daughter of Dr Austin Sloper, a brilliant, sarcastic physician who has never forgiven her for not being like her beautiful, dead mother. When the charming but penniless Morris Townsend begins to court her, her father is sure he is after her inheritance and forbids the marriage, while her romantic aunt Lavinia Penniman encourages the affair. Catherine must find out what she herself wants.
context: Henry James published this short novel in 1880, building it from an anecdote told to him by the actress Fanny Kemble. Spare and ironic, with a quiet heroine who turns out to be unexpectedly strong, it is one of his most accessible books; the stage and film versions are called The Heiress. Continue with [The Portrait of a Lady](/book/352?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/jamesh?lang=en).

about: In the Swiss resort of Vevey, Frederick Winterbourne, an American who has lived in Europe so long that he has almost forgotten America, meets Daisy Miller, a pretty, lively young woman from Schenectady, New York, travelling with her mother and her little brother. Daisy talks to anyone, goes out without a chaperone and ignores what people think. Winterbourne cannot decide whether she is innocent or shameless, and when they meet again in Rome, where she is seen everywhere with a handsome Italian, the American colony turns its back on her.
context: Published in 1878, Daisy Miller was Henry James's first great popular success and created a type: the free, innocent American girl misjudged by old Europe. It can be read in an evening. Read [Washington Square](/book/3001?lang=en) next, and see [his life](/author/jamesh?lang=en).

about: Tristram Shandy sets out to tell his life and opinions, but he is so distracted by digressions that he takes an extraordinarily long time even to get himself born. Instead we meet his father Walter, full of strange theories about names and noses; his gentle uncle Toby, wounded at the siege of Namur, who spends his days rebuilding battlefields on the bowling green with his servant Corporal Trim; and the melancholy parson Yorick. The book includes a black page, a marbled page, a blank page for the reader's own drawing and chapters out of order.
context: Laurence Sterne (1713–1768), a Yorkshire clergyman, published it in nine volumes between 1759 and 1767 and became famous overnight. Two centuries before modernism, it played games with time, memory and the very form of the novel, and writers from James Joyce to Salman Rushdie have learned from it. Compare a more conventional novel of its age, [Tom Jones](/book/6598?lang=en).

about: Paris, 1640. Cyrano de Bergerac is a poet, a soldier of the Gascon cadets and the finest swordsman in France, who can compose a ballade while fighting a duel, but he has an enormous nose and believes no woman could love him. He loves his beautiful cousin Roxane, who loves the handsome young cadet Christian, and Christian has no gift for words. So Cyrano writes Christian's love letters for him, and even whispers the words under Roxane's balcony at night.
context: Edmond Rostand (1868–1918) based his hero on a real seventeenth-century writer, Savinien de Cyrano de Bergerac, who wrote comic fantasies about journeys to the Moon. The verse play's first night in Paris, in December 1897, was a triumph, and it remains one of the most performed of all French plays. Cyrano's speech mocking his own nose is a showpiece for actors.

about: Three friends, the narrator J., George and Harris, decide they are suffering from overwork and need a rest. Rejecting a sea voyage, they take a boat up the River Thames from Kingston towards Oxford, together with Montmorency, a fox terrier with a talent for trouble. The trip is a chain of small disasters: a tin of pineapple and no tin-opener, a tow line that tangles itself, an ambitious Irish stew, and memories of Harris getting lost in the maze at Hampton Court.
context: Jerome K. Jerome (1859–1927) set out to write a serious guide to the Thames, with notes on its history, and some of those passages remain, but the comedy took over. Published in 1889, the book has never been out of print and is still one of the funniest in English; the narrator's opening discovery, from a medical dictionary, that he has every disease except housemaid's knee is famous.

about: George F. Babbitt is a forty-six-year-old real estate agent in the booming Midwestern city of Zenith. He owns a modern house, a car and every new gadget, belongs to the right clubs, gives speeches about pep and progress and believes whatever his newspaper tells him. Yet beneath his satisfaction he feels a vague, aching emptiness, and when his closest friend's life falls apart he attempts his own small rebellion against the rules of his world, and discovers what it costs.
context: Published in 1922, two years after [Main Street](/book/842?lang=en), Sinclair Lewis's satire of business culture was so recognisable that 'Babbitt' entered the dictionary as a word for a self-satisfied, conformist businessman. In 1930 Lewis became the first American to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. The book's portrait of advertising, boosterism and the fear of standing out still feels current.

about: What is the good life? Aristotle answers that everyone seeks happiness, eudaimonia, and that it lies not in pleasure, wealth or honour but in activity in accordance with virtue, over a whole life. He explains virtue as a habit formed by practice, a mean between two extremes, as courage lies between cowardice and recklessness, and goes on to discuss justice, practical wisdom, self-control and friendship, which fills two of the ten books, ending with the life of contemplation.
context: Named after Aristotle's son Nicomachus, who may have edited it, the work probably grew from his lectures at the Lyceum in Athens in the fourth century BC. It was central to ethics in the Islamic world, where Ibn Rushd (Averroes) wrote a commentary on it, and in medieval Europe, and it is widely read again today. It leads on to his [Politics](/book/84?lang=en); see [his life](/author/aristotle?lang=en).

about: This small book of spiritual advice, written in short chapters and brief sayings, teaches the reader to turn away from vanity, ambition and the love of praise, to bear suffering patiently, to know oneself honestly and to seek God in silence and humility. Its four books move from general counsel on the spiritual life to the inner life, to inward consolation and finally to the sacrament of the Eucharist.
context: It is traditionally attributed to Thomas à Kempis (about 1380–1471), a German-born monk who spent most of his long life copying manuscripts in a monastery near Zwolle in the Netherlands, and it grew out of the Devotio Moderna, a movement of simple, practical piety. Written in Latin in the early fifteenth century, it became, after the Bible, one of the most widely read Christian books, treasured by readers as different as Ignatius of Loyola and John Wesley.

about: On a diplomatic mission to Flanders in 1515, Thomas More meets a well-travelled scholar, Raphael Hythloday, who has sailed with Amerigo Vespucci and lived for five years on a distant island called Utopia. In the first part they discuss the injustices of England, where thieves are hanged while sheep, as Hythloday puts it, devour men, as farmland is enclosed for wool; in the second he describes Utopia, where there is no private property, everyone works six hours a day, gold is used for chamber pots and chains, and religious tolerance is law.
context: Written in Latin and published in 1516, the book gave the world the word 'utopia', a Greek pun meaning both 'no place' and 'good place'. Thomas More (1478–1535) later became Lord Chancellor of England and was executed for refusing to accept Henry VIII as head of the Church. Compare [Plato's Republic](/book/74?lang=en).

about: From 431 to 404 BC, Athens and Sparta, the two great powers of Greece, fought a long and ruinous war. Thucydides, an Athenian general exiled after failing to save the city of Amphipolis, used his exile to write its history, questioning witnesses on both sides. His book contains Pericles' funeral oration in praise of Athenian democracy, the plague that struck Athens, which he survived, the brutal Melian dialogue, in which Athens tells a small island that 'the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must', and the disastrous expedition to Sicily.
context: Thucydides (about 460–400 BC) set out to write not entertaining stories but 'a possession for all time', based on evidence and a cold analysis of power, and he is often called the father of political realism. His account breaks off in 411 BC, unfinished. See [his life](/author/thucydides?lang=en).

about: 'Man is only a reed, the weakest thing in nature, but he is a thinking reed.' These are the notes Blaise Pascal left for a great defence of Christianity that he never finished: fragments on the misery and greatness of human beings, on our endless need for distraction, on the limits of reason, and the famous wager, which argues that a sensible person should bet on God's existence because there is everything to gain and little to lose. 'The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.'
context: Pascal (1623–1662) was a mathematical genius who built one of the first calculating machines as a young man, studied the vacuum and helped found probability theory, before a mystical experience in 1654 turned him wholly to religion. He died at thirty-nine, and the fragments were published in 1670. Readers of any belief find his aphorisms startlingly modern.

about: How can we settle philosophical arguments that seem endless? William James proposes a simple test: ask what practical difference it would make if one view or the other were true; if none, the dispute is empty. He starts with a playful quarrel about whether a man walking round a tree goes 'round' a squirrel that keeps to the far side of the trunk. In eight lectures, given in Boston and New York in 1906 and 1907, he applies the method to God, free will and truth itself.
context: James (1842–1910), brother of the novelist Henry James, trained as a doctor and set up one of the first psychology laboratories in America, at Harvard, before turning to philosophy. Written with warmth and humour, the book made pragmatism, a word taken from his friend Charles Sanders Peirce, the best-known American philosophy. See also [The Varieties of Religious Experience](/book/384?lang=en) and [his life](/author/james?lang=en).

about: Einstein wrote this little book in 1916 for readers who know school mathematics but not the advanced kind, to explain his two theories in his own words. He begins with simple questions, such as what it means to say that two lightning strikes far apart along a railway happen at the same moment. Using trains, embankments and a chest pulled through empty space, he shows why time and distance depend on the motion of the observer, why nothing can outrun light, and how gravity reshapes space and time.
context: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was a patent clerk in Bern when he published special relativity in 1905; general relativity followed in 1915, and its prediction that light bends near the Sun was confirmed during an eclipse in 1919, which made him world famous. His Nobel Prize, for 1921, was given not for relativity but for his work on the photoelectric effect.

about: Is there any knowledge so certain that no reasonable person could doubt it? Bertrand Russell begins with the table in front of him, which looks different in colour and shape to every observer, and asks what we really know about it. In fifteen short chapters, written for general readers, he moves from appearance and reality to idealism, knowledge by acquaintance and by description, induction and truth, and ends with the value of philosophy, which lies, he argues, in its very uncertainty.
context: Russell (1872–1970), British mathematician, philosopher and campaigner for peace, wrote the book in 1912, while he and Alfred North Whitehead were publishing Principia Mathematica. It is still one of the best introductions to philosophy, and Russell received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950. For an older classic on the same questions, see [Hume's Enquiry](/book/277?lang=en).

about: On a bleak December midnight, a lonely scholar sits over old books mourning his lost love, Lenore, when he hears a tapping at his chamber door. A raven steps in, perches on a bust of Pallas above the door and answers every question with one word: 'Nevermore'. As his questions grow more desperate, the bird's single reply drives him into despair.
context: Edgar Allan Poe published the poem in January 1845, and it made him famous almost overnight, though he earned very little from it. In his essay 'The Philosophy of Composition' he claimed he had built it step by step, like a problem in mathematics, choosing the word 'Nevermore' for its sound and the death of a beautiful woman as the most poetic of subjects. Read his stories, starting with [The Fall of the House of Usher](/book/128?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/poe?lang=en).

about: In August 1889, eighteen-year-old Caroline Meeber leaves her small Wisconsin town for Chicago with a little money and a great hunger for fine clothes and a better life. Work in a shoe factory is exhausting and badly paid, and she drifts into the protection of Drouet, a cheerful travelling salesman, and then of George Hurstwood, the manager of a fashionable saloon, who steals money from his employers and flees with her to New York. As Carrie rises, Hurstwood sinks.
context: Theodore Dreiser (1871–1945), from a poor German immigrant family in Indiana, published his first novel in 1900, and its publisher barely promoted it, reportedly because Carrie is never punished for her 'sins'. It is now seen as a landmark of American realism, showing people driven by desire and money rather than by morals. Compare a European heroine with similar dreams, [Madame Bovary](/book/324?lang=en).

about: 'This is the saddest story I have ever heard,' begins John Dowell, a wealthy American who for nine years spent his summers at a German spa with his wife Florence and an English couple: Captain Edward Ashburnham, an apparently perfect gentleman and soldier, and his wife Leonora. The four seemed the best of friends. Only after Florence's death does Dowell begin to discover what was really happening, and as he tells the story out of order, circling back and contradicting himself, the reader starts to wonder how much he understood, or chose not to see.
context: Ford Madox Ford (1873–1939), English novelist and editor, who wrote two novels together with [Joseph Conrad](/author/conrad?lang=en), published the book in 1915 and considered it his best. It is a masterpiece of the unreliable narrator, as carefully built as a detective story.

about: A newspaper editor in India tells how he met two loafers, Daniel Dravot and Peachey Carnehan, former soldiers who have signed a contract forbidding drink and women until their plan is complete: to travel into the mountains of Kafiristan, beyond Afghanistan, with twenty rifles, and make themselves kings. Two years later a broken, crippled man stumbles into the editor's office at night to tell him what happened.
context: Rudyard Kipling wrote the story in 1888, when he was twenty-two and working as a journalist in India, and it remains one of the great tales of ambition and empire. John Huston's 1975 film with Sean Connery and Michael Caine brought it new readers. Read [Kim](/book/356?lang=en) next, and see [Kipling's life](/author/kipling?lang=en).

about: An old sailor with a glittering eye stops one of three young men on his way to a wedding feast and, holding him spellbound, tells his tale. Driven by storms to the icy south, his ship was led out of the fog by an albatross, which he shot with his crossbow for no reason. As punishment, the ship is becalmed under a burning sun, with 'water, water, every where, nor any drop to drink', his shipmates die one by one, and the dead albatross is hung around his neck.
context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote the poem in 1797 and 1798, and it opened [Lyrical Ballads](/book/291?lang=en), the book he published with William Wordsworth that launched English Romanticism. Its strange images, the phantom ship and the water-snakes the mariner blesses 'unaware', have stayed with readers ever since, and 'an albatross around one's neck' has entered the language.

about: These two sets of short poems show, in Blake's own words, 'the two contrary states of the human soul'. The Songs of Innocence speak with the voice of childhood: a lamb, a shepherd, a laughing song, an echoing green, and a little chimney sweeper who still dreams of an angel. The Songs of Experience answer them with fear, injustice and repression: the fierce 'Tyger, tyger, burning bright', the sick rose, and the 'mind-forg'd manacles' heard in every street of London.
context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London engraver who printed these poems himself, in 1789 and 1794, etching words and pictures together on copper plates and colouring each copy by hand with his wife Catherine, so no two copies are alike. Almost unknown in his lifetime, he is now counted among the great English poets and artists. For other early Romantics, see [Lyrical Ballads](/book/291?lang=en).

about: 'April is the cruellest month,' begins this poem in five parts, which moves through a broken modern world of voices: a fortune-teller with a wicked pack of cards, a nervous woman in a rich room, two women gossiping in a London pub at closing time, a typist and her careless lover, crowds flowing over London Bridge, 'so many, I had not thought death had undone so many', and finally thunder over a dry land in the East. Fragments of Dante, Shakespeare, the Buddha and the Upanishads are woven together.
context: T. S. Eliot (1888–1965), an American who settled in London, published the poem in 1922, after his friend Ezra Pound helped cut it down, and it became the defining poem of modernism; Eliot received the Nobel Prize in 1948. It is difficult, but it rewards being read aloud, and Eliot added his own notes. Read his earlier [Prufrock](/book/1682?lang=en) first.

about: 'Let us go then, you and I, when the evening is spread out against the sky like a patient etherised upon a table.' The first poem of this slim book follows J. Alfred Prufrock, a timid, ageing man, through foggy streets to a drawing room where women 'come and go, talking of Michelangelo', as he wonders whether he dares ask an 'overwhelming question' and fears he has 'measured out my life with coffee spoons'. The other poems include 'Portrait of a Lady', 'Preludes' and 'Rhapsody on a Windy Night'.
context: T. S. Eliot was twenty-eight when this, his first book, appeared in London in 1917, two years after Ezra Pound arranged the publication of 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' in a Chicago magazine. Its ironic, conversational voice and images of the modern city changed English poetry. Continue with [The Waste Land](/book/1549?lang=en).

about: Born into slavery in Edenton, North Carolina, Harriet Jacobs tells her story under the name Linda Brent. As a girl she is pursued for years by her master, Dr Flint, who is determined to make her submit to him, and she tries to protect herself through a relationship with another white man, with whom she has two children. To escape Flint and save her children, she hides for almost seven years in a tiny crawl space above a shed at her grandmother's house, too low to stand in, before escaping to the North.
context: Jacobs (1813–1897) published the book in 1861 with the help of the abolitionist Lydia Maria Child. For a long time it was thought to be a novel, until the historian Jean Fagan Yellin showed in the 1980s that its main events were true. It is one of the most important accounts of what slavery did to women. Read it with [Frederick Douglass's Narrative](/book/403?lang=en).

about: Solomon Northup was a free Black man, a husband, father and violinist living in Saratoga Springs, New York. In 1841 two men offered him work with a travelling circus and took him to Washington, where he was drugged, chained and sold into slavery. Renamed Platt, he spent twelve years on plantations in Louisiana, picking cotton and cutting sugar cane under masters both kind and brutal, until a Canadian carpenter agreed to carry a letter north for him.
context: Written with the help of a white lawyer, David Wilson, the narrative was published in 1853, months after Northup regained his freedom, and sold widely as the quarrel over slavery grew fiercer. Historians value it for its precise detail about plantation life, and the 2013 film based on it won the Oscar for Best Picture. Northup dedicated it to Harriet Beecher Stowe; read it with her [Uncle Tom's Cabin](/book/522?lang=en).

about: In a sacred grove at Nemi, near Rome, there was once a strange rule: the priest of the goddess Diana could be replaced only by a runaway slave who broke a branch from a certain tree and then killed him. Starting from this puzzle, James Frazer gathers customs from every continent, from rain-making and taboos to the killing of divine kings and the festivals of dying and reviving gods, to argue that human thought develops from magic through religion to science.
context: Frazer (1854–1941), a Scottish scholar who did his research in Cambridge libraries rather than in the field, first published the book in two volumes in 1890, expanded it to twelve, and then made a famous one-volume abridgement in 1922. Many of its theories are now rejected, but it deeply influenced writers such as T. S. Eliot, whose notes to [The Waste Land](/book/1549?lang=en) cite it.

about: The novel opens with a mother writing a letter on a beach in Cornwall, her tears blurring the bay, while her small son Jacob wanders off and finds a sheep's jaw in the sand. We follow Jacob Flanders through boyhood, Cambridge, love affairs in London and a journey to Greece, but always from the outside, in brief glimpses and the impressions he leaves on others, as if the narrator can never quite reach him.
context: Virginia Woolf (1882–1941) published the novel in 1922 through the Hogarth Press, which she ran with her husband Leonard, and it was her first truly experimental book. Jacob was partly inspired by her brother Thoby, who died young, and the last pages quietly reveal the shadow of the First World War. It leads straight to [Mrs Dalloway](/book/348?lang=en); see [her life](/author/woolf?lang=en).

about: Rachel Vinrace, twenty-four, sheltered and musical, sails from London to South America on her father's ship with her aunt Helen Ambrose, who decides to take charge of her education. At a hotel in a small resort, among a group of English tourists, Rachel meets Terence Hewet, a young man who wants to write a novel about silence, and on a river journey into the jungle she begins to discover love and her own mind.
context: Published in 1915 after years of rewriting, this was Virginia Woolf's first novel, more traditional in form than her later books but already full of her questions about women's freedom and inner life. Richard and Clarissa Dalloway appear briefly on the ship, ten years before [Mrs Dalloway](/book/348?lang=en). See [her life](/author/woolf?lang=en).

about: In the town of Chandrapore under British rule, Adela Quested arrives from England with Mrs Moore, the mother of the man she may marry, hoping to see 'the real India'. A warm-hearted Muslim doctor, Aziz, befriends them and arranges an outing to the famous Marabar Caves, but in one of the echoing caves something happens to Adela, or she believes it does, and Aziz is arrested for assaulting her. The trial divides the town between Indians and English, with the college principal Fielding caught in the middle.
context: E. M. Forster visited India twice and worked for a time as secretary to an Indian maharaja, and he published the novel in 1924. Its question, whether friendship between an Englishman and an Indian is possible under empire, made it one of the great novels of the twentieth century, and David Lean filmed it in 1984. Compare Forster's earlier [Howards End](/book/3074?lang=en).

about: Across three generations, the Brangwen family farms the Marsh Farm on the border of Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire, while the industrial world spreads around them. Tom Brangwen marries a Polish widow, Lydia; her daughter Anna marries Tom's nephew Will in a stormy, passionate marriage; and their daughter Ursula, the book's true heroine, struggles as a teacher in a harsh school, goes to university and refuses the life planned for women.
context: D. H. Lawrence published the novel in 1915; within weeks it was prosecuted for obscenity, and about a thousand copies were destroyed. Today it is seen as one of his finest books. Ursula's story continues in [Women in Love](/book/4324?lang=en); see also [Sons and Lovers](/book/354?lang=en) and [his life](/author/lawrence?lang=en).

about: At a country fair, a young hay-trusser named Michael Henchard gets drunk on rum-laced furmity and sells his wife and baby daughter to a sailor for five guineas. Waking sober and ashamed, he swears not to touch drink for twenty-one years. Years later his wife returns with her daughter and finds him a prosperous corn merchant and the mayor of Casterbridge. But Henchard's pride, his temper and the past he cannot bury slowly destroy everything he has built.
context: Thomas Hardy published the novel in 1886; Casterbridge is his portrait of Dorchester, the Dorset market town where he lived. Henchard, a man of great strength and greater flaws, is one of the most tragic figures in Victorian fiction, a King Lear of the corn market. Read also [Tess of the d'Urbervilles](/book/306?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/hardy?lang=en).

about: On Egdon Heath, a wild stretch of Wessex moorland, the restless and beautiful Eustacia Vye longs to escape to the brilliant life of Paris. When Clym Yeobright, a native of the heath, comes home from a successful career in the diamond trade in Paris, she sees him as her way out, while Clym dreams only of staying and becoming a teacher to the poor people of the heath. Their marriage, and the jealousies around them, lead to tragedy.
context: Published in 1878, the novel opens with a famous chapter that describes the heath itself as a living, brooding presence. Thomas Hardy grew up at the edge of such heathland in Dorset, and the book's bonfires, storms and Gothic atmosphere make it one of his most memorable. See [The Mayor of Casterbridge](/book/488?lang=en) and [his life](/author/hardy?lang=en).

about: In 1745, when Bonnie Prince Charlie rises against the crown, the Durie family of Durrisdeer in Scotland decides to keep a son on each side. The brilliant, charming and wicked elder brother James, the Master of Ballantrae, joins the rebellion, while the dull, decent Henry stays at home loyal to King George. James is reported dead at Culloden, and Henry inherits his place and marries the woman James was to marry, but the Master returns, again and again, from exile, piracy and India, to torment him.
context: Published in 1889, the novel is told mostly by the family's loyal steward, Mackellar, who is not as neutral as he believes. It is one of Robert Louis Stevenson's darkest and most ambitious books, a tale of two brothers that ranges from Scotland to the wilderness of New York. Read also [Kidnapped](/book/187?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/stevenson?lang=en).

about: In 1665 the Great Plague killed perhaps a hundred thousand people in London. This book is presented as the memoir of a saddler, known only by the initials H. F., who stays in the city while the rich flee, and walks its emptying streets. He records the weekly bills of mortality, houses shut up with their sick families inside and a red cross on the door, the dead-carts and plague pits, quacks selling useless cures, and moments of courage, panic and cruelty.
context: Daniel Defoe was only about five during the plague, and he published the book in 1722, when Londoners feared that a plague then raging in Marseille would reach them. It mixes real records with invented scenes so skilfully that it was long read as true history, and it found many new readers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Read [Robinson Crusoe](/book/300?lang=en), and see [Defoe's life](/author/defoe?lang=en).

about: A man named Christian, weighed down by a heavy burden on his back and terrified by the book he is reading, leaves the City of Destruction and sets out for the Celestial City. On his journey, told as a dream, he falls into the Slough of Despond, loses his burden at the foot of the Cross, fights the monster Apollyon, passes through the Valley of the Shadow of Death, is arrested with his friend Faithful at Vanity Fair, and is locked in Doubting Castle by Giant Despair.
context: John Bunyan (1628–1688), a tinker and Puritan preacher, began the book while imprisoned in Bedford for preaching without a licence, and published it in 1678. For centuries it was, after the Bible, the most read book in English homes, and names such as Vanity Fair and the Slough of Despond have entered everyday language. Bunyan later added a second part, about the journey of Christian's wife, Christiana.

about: Dr Charles Primrose, a kind, simple and slightly vain country clergyman, tells the story of his family: his wife Deborah, who has social ambitions, his sons George and Moses, and his daughters Olivia and Sophia. When the merchant holding his savings goes bankrupt, the family moves to a poorer parish, where the handsome young squire Thornhill seduces Olivia, and misfortune follows misfortune, from a fire to a debtors' prison, while the vicar keeps his faith and his humour. Moses, sent to sell a horse at the fair, comes back with a gross of green spectacles.
context: Oliver Goldsmith (about 1728–1774), an Irish writer in London, was facing arrest for debt when his friend Samuel Johnson sold the manuscript to pay his rent; it was published in 1766. Gentle and comic, it was one of the most loved novels for a century, admired by Goethe and mentioned in Jane Austen's [Emma](/book/39?lang=en).

about: The Caliph Vathek, grandson of Harun al-Rashid, is a ruler of enormous appetites who has built five palaces dedicated to the five senses and a tower from which to study the stars. When a hideous stranger, the Giaour, promises him the treasures of the pre-Adamite sultans, Vathek, urged on by his mother Carathis, a sorceress, commits crime after crime and sets out with the beautiful Nouronihar for the ruins of Istakhar and the underground halls of Eblis (Iblis).
context: William Beckford (1760–1844), one of the richest men in England, wrote this Oriental tale in French when he was about twenty-one, in three days and two nights, he later claimed; an English translation appeared in 1786. Inspired by the Arabian Nights, it mixes comedy, cruelty and nightmare, and its vision of the halls of Eblis impressed Byron. Compare [The Arabian Nights](/book/479?lang=en) and the Gothic [Castle of Otranto](/book/983?lang=en).

about: Little Nell Trent, a gentle girl not yet fourteen, lives with her grandfather among the dusty antiques of his curiosity shop in London. Secretly the old man is a gambler, losing everything in the hope of making her rich, and he falls into the power of Daniel Quilp, a grotesque and cruel dwarf who lends money. Ruined, Nell and her grandfather flee the city and wander the roads of England, meeting Punch-and-Judy men, a travelling waxwork show and strangers both kind and wicked, while Quilp and others try to track them down.
context: Charles Dickens published the novel in weekly parts in 1840 and 1841, and readers became so attached to Nell that its sales reportedly reached a hundred thousand copies a week. It also introduced two of his most delightful comic characters, the idle Dick Swiveller and the half-starved servant he names the Marchioness. Read [Great Expectations](/book/29?lang=en), and see [Dickens's life](/author/dickens?lang=en).

about: A boatman, Gaffer Hexam, and his daughter Lizzie row on the Thames at night searching for drowned bodies, and they find one identified as John Harmon, heir to a fortune made from London's mountains of rubbish. Harmon was to inherit on condition of marrying Bella Wilfer, a pretty, money-minded girl he had never met. With him apparently dead, the money goes to the kind, simple dustman Mr Boffin and his wife, who take Bella into their home, while a reserved young man named John Rokesmith becomes Boffin's secretary.
context: Dickens's last completed novel, published in monthly parts in 1864 and 1865, is a dark, rich satire of a society obsessed with money, full of memorable characters such as the social-climbing Veneerings and Jenny Wren, the doll's dressmaker. While writing it Dickens survived a terrible railway crash at Staplehurst, with part of the manuscript in his coat. See [his life](/author/dickens?lang=en).

about: When his father dies penniless, nineteen-year-old Nicholas Nickleby, with his mother and sister Kate, turns for help to his rich uncle Ralph, a cold-hearted moneylender, who sends him to teach at Dotheboys Hall, a Yorkshire school run by the brutal, one-eyed Wackford Squeers, where unwanted boys are starved and beaten. Nicholas rebels, thrashes Squeers and escapes with Smike, a broken young drudge, and they join a travelling theatre company before returning to London to protect Kate from his uncle's schemes.
context: Charles Dickens visited Yorkshire schools under a false name before writing the novel, published in 1838 and 1839, and his portrait of Squeers helped bring such schools to an end. Full of comedy, including the theatrical Crummles family, it was his third novel, after [Oliver Twist](/book/31?lang=en). See [his life](/author/dickens?lang=en).

about: Paul Dombey, a proud, cold London merchant, cares about one thing: that his firm should be 'Dombey and Son'. When his wife dies giving birth to the long-awaited son, little Paul, he pours all his hopes into the frail boy and coldly ignores his loving daughter Florence. The story follows the family through grief, a disastrous second marriage to the haughty Edith Granger and the fall of the firm, while Florence goes on hoping for her father's love.
context: Published in monthly parts from 1846 to 1848, Dombey and Son is often seen as the first novel Dickens carefully planned around a single theme, pride, and it vividly captures the railways that were then tearing through London's old streets. Read also [David Copperfield](/book/32?lang=en), which followed it, and see [his life](/author/dickens?lang=en).

about: Agnes Grey, the younger daughter of a poor clergyman, decides to help her family by becoming a governess. Her first post is with the Bloomfields, whose spoiled children torment animals and their teacher while their parents blame her for everything; her second is with the Murrays, whose vain elder daughter Rosalie collects admirers. Quiet and lonely, Agnes finds comfort in the kindness of the new curate, Mr Weston.
context: Anne Brontë (1820–1849), the youngest of the Brontë sisters, drew on her own unhappy years as a governess, and the novel was published in 1847, the same year as her sisters' [Jane Eyre](/book/304?lang=en) and [Wuthering Heights](/book/305?lang=en). Calm, honest and quietly ironic, it was long overshadowed by them. Read her bolder [The Tenant of Wildfell Hall](/book/1230?lang=en) next.

about: A mysterious young woman, Mrs Helen Graham, said to be a widow, moves into the half-ruined old house of Wildfell Hall with her little son and earns her living as a painter, and the neighbourhood soon fills with gossip about her.
